titre: No One Had Thought of Drawing Numbers Before Him
accroche: In 1786, a penniless Scottish engineer has the idea that seems obvious today: replacing tables of figures with lines and bars.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1786, the Scottish engineer and economist William Playfair publishes *The Commercial and Political Atlas* in London. The book gathers forty-three line and shaded-area graphs, tracing the evolution of British foreign trade in the 18th century, plus one isolated graph, different from the others: a vertical bar chart comparing Scottish exports to seventeen countries. Nothing like it had existed before in such a systematic form. Playfair invents, in the same book, two of the three statistical graphs most used still today, two centuries later.

## Seeing a Curve Rather Than Reading a Table

Playfair's idea starts from a simple observation: a table of figures requires comparing columns one by one, whereas a curve shows an entire trend at a single glance. On one of his most cited graphs, two lines trace respectively England's imports and exports with Denmark and Norway, year by year from 1700 to 1780; the shaded area between the two lines, depending on whether it leans one way or the other, directly indicates whether the trade balance is favorable or in deficit, information that previously had to be calculated column after column, country by country. Fifteen years later, in the 1801 *Statistical Breviary*, Playfair goes further: to compare the area of the Ottoman Empire divided among Europe, Asia, and Africa, he invents a new format, a circle cut into colored slices proportional to each continent, the first pie chart ever published, in a book otherwise devoted to comparing, plate after plate, the area, population, and military power of the great European nations.

## An Inventor Who Died Unrecognized

Playfair dies on February 11, 1823, in Covent Garden, at sixty-three, without his inventions having earned him recognition in his lifetime. Historians of science now describe him as the author of the greatest leap forward in the history of graphic representation, yet he remained obscure until the 20th century, when his work was rediscovered and republished. It is only after his death that his three inventions spread separately, each carried by different uses: the line in science and economics, the bar in official statistics, the circle in popularization, to the point that today, most readers of a pie chart do not know that it bears the mark of a single man, and of a single book.

repere.texte: In his Statistical Breviary (1801), William Playfair publishes the very first pie chart in history: a circle cut into three colored slices, proportional to the area of the Ottoman Empire in Europe, in Asia, and in Africa.

carte.punch: In 1801, William Playfair cuts the area of the Ottoman Empire into colored slices of a circle.
carte.idee: In 1786, the Scottish engineer William Playfair publishes line graphs and a bar chart on British trade. In 1801, he invents the pie chart. He dies in 1823 without his inventions having earned him recognition in his lifetime.

quiz.question: What did William Playfair invent first, in his 1786 Commercial and Political Atlas?
choix: The pie chart, to compare an empire's area by continent
The histogram, to represent the distribution of British incomes
The line graph and the bar chart, to represent the evolution of foreign trade
The scatter plot, to compare two economic variables with each other
quiz.explication: The 1786 Atlas introduces the line graph, across forty-three graphs devoted to foreign trade, and a vertical bar chart. The pie chart does not appear until fifteen years later, in 1801, in the Statistical Breviary, not in the Atlas.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the 1801 Statistical Breviary, what does the size of the circles drawn by Playfair represent?
choix: The population of each country compared
The area of each country, with population indicated separately
The trade revenue of each country compared
The number of inhabitants per square kilometer of each country
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The introduction to the Statistical Breviary specifies that the size of the circles encodes area, with population and revenue shown separately by colored lines.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the isolated graph in the 1786 Atlas, different from the other forty-three?
choix: A pie chart comparing the population of seventeen countries
A scatter plot comparing wheat prices over a century
A bar chart comparing Scottish exports to seventeen countries
A map of British maritime trade in the Mediterranean
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of the Atlas's forty-four graphs, forty-three are line graphs; the only other one is a vertical bar chart comparing Scottish exports to seventeen countries.
